plan: Natural-science passage of about 650 words (CLD-P-ACT-R-000013) on masting, following the Reading audit's mitigation: three items connect distant paragraphs, near-miss distractors (reversed roles, earlier view restated, specialists described in other words).

passages.title: The Mast Year
passages.text:
In some autumns the ground beneath a stand of oaks is nearly bare. In others, acorns lie so thick that walking on them feels like walking on marbles. Ecologists call these sudden, synchronized bumper crops "mast years," and for most of the twentieth century they treated them largely as a matter of weather: a warm spring and a wet summer produced a large crop, and a late frost or a drought produced a small one.

The weather explanation has an obvious appeal, and it is not wrong so much as incomplete. Weather does affect seed production. But if weather were the whole story, the size of a crop should track the quality of the growing season fairly closely, and it does not. Researchers who compared decades of seed counts with climate records found mast years following ordinary summers and poor crops following excellent ones. More puzzling still, trees of the same species hundreds of kilometers apart, growing under different local conditions, often mast in the same year. Whatever coordinates them, it seems to be more than the weather each tree happens to experience.

One alternative begins not with the trees but with the animals that eat their seeds. A squirrel or a weevil that depends on acorns can multiply only as fast as its food supply allows. If oaks produced a steady, moderate crop every year, seed eaters would settle at a population large enough to consume most of it. By producing almost nothing for several years and then a flood of seeds all at once, the trees starve their predators down and then overwhelm them: in a mast year there are simply too few mouths to eat everything, and many seeds survive to sprout. This idea, known as predator satiation, predicts that masting should be most pronounced in species whose seeds are eaten by specialists, animals that depend heavily on that one food, a pattern that several studies have reported.

A second explanation concerns pollination. Oaks, like many masting trees, are pollinated by wind, an inefficient method in which most pollen never reaches a flower. When many trees flower heavily in the same year, the air is thick with pollen and a larger share of flowers are fertilized. A tree that flowered heavily on its own, out of step with its neighbors, would waste much of the effort.

Neither explanation tells us how trees spread across a region manage to act together. Here weather may return, though in a different role. A tree that has spent several years storing resources may need only a cue, such as an unusually warm early summer, to commit those resources to flowers. Because a single weather pattern can cover a large region, it can serve as a signal that many trees respond to at once, even if it is not, by itself, the reason they produce so many seeds.

The emerging picture, then, is not a choice between weather and strategy but a division of labor between them. Stored resources determine whether a tree is able to mast; weather often determines when; and the benefits of satiating predators and improving pollination help explain why trees that mast together have prospered. It is an arrangement that no single tree designed, but one that the forest, over many generations, has come to depend on.

candidates.stem: The main purpose of the passage is to argue that mast years are best explained by:

choices.A: seed predators alone, since weather has little real effect on crop size.
choices.B: several factors acting together, with weather often setting the timing.
choices.C: the need of wind-pollinated trees to improve the efficiency of pollination.
choices.D: the quality of each tree's growing season, as earlier ecologists believed.

candidates.evidence: a division of labor between them
candidates.explanation: The final paragraph sums up: stored resources, weather as a timing cue, and the benefits of predator satiation and pollination together explain masting.

A.rationale: The author says weather "does affect seed production" and gives it a role in timing.

C.rationale: Pollination is one of several factors, not the whole explanation.

D.rationale: The author calls this view incomplete and argues against relying on it alone.

hints: Read the final paragraph: how many factors does it name?

strategy.explanation: Summarize the conclusion before reading the choices.

candidates.remember: A main claim usually appears in summary form near the end.

candidates.subskill: Comparing two roles for the same factor
candidates.stem: Compared with the view described in the first paragraph, the role the author gives weather in the fifth paragraph is best described as:

choices.A: a minor factor that the author finally rejects as having no bearing on masting at all.
choices.B: the main reason trees produce bumper crops, just as ecologists long believed.
choices.C: a factor that matters only in wind-pollinated species such as the oaks in the passage.
choices.D: a cue that tells many trees when to spend stored resources, not the main cause of a large crop.

candidates.evidence: even if it is not, by itself, the reason they produce so many seeds
candidates.explanation: In paragraph 1 weather is treated as the cause of crop size. In paragraph 5 it becomes a regional signal for when trees commit stored resources, "not, by itself, the reason they produce so many seeds."

A.rationale: The author keeps weather in the explanation, as a signal for timing.

B.rationale: That is the first paragraph's view, which the author revises.

C.rationale: Paragraph 5 does not limit weather's role to wind-pollinated trees.

hints: How did ecologists see weather in paragraph 1?
What does "in a different role" in paragraph 5 suggest?

strategy.explanation: Compare paragraph 1 with the last sentence of paragraph 5.

candidates.remember: When a factor "returns," ask how its role has changed.

author_checklist.hardness: Requires connecting paragraphs 1 and 5; choice C restates the earlier view the author revises.

candidates.stem: The author mentions that trees "hundreds of kilometers apart" often mast in the same year (paragraph 2) mainly to:

choices.A: suggest that something beyond each tree's local weather coordinates masting.
choices.B: show that weather has no effect on how many seeds a tree produces.
choices.C: support the idea that predator satiation is the full explanation for masting.
choices.D: illustrate how far seed-eating animals travel in search of acorns.

candidates.evidence: Whatever coordinates them, it seems to be more than the weather each tree happens to experience
candidates.explanation: Distant trees under different local conditions still mast together, so local weather alone cannot explain the synchrony.

B.rationale: The paragraph says weather "does affect seed production."

C.rationale: Predator satiation is not introduced until paragraph 3.

D.rationale: The detail concerns trees, not how far animals travel.

hints: Why is it puzzling that distant trees mast together?

strategy.explanation: Read the sentence after the detail.

candidates.remember: Evidence questions: ask what claim the detail supports.

candidates.stem: Based on paragraph 3, masting would be expected to be LEAST pronounced in a tree species whose seeds are eaten mainly by:

choices.A: weevils that feed almost entirely on that species' seeds.
choices.B: squirrels whose numbers rise and fall with the size of the crop.
choices.C: animals that also eat many other kinds of food.
choices.D: a beetle that lays its eggs only inside those seeds.

candidates.evidence: masting should be most pronounced in species whose seeds are eaten by specialists
candidates.explanation: Predator satiation works by starving down predators that depend on one food. Animals with many other foods are not starved down in lean years, so masting would help least and be least pronounced.

A.rationale: Weevils that rely on one food are specialists, where masting should be most pronounced.

B.rationale: Predators that track the crop are the ones masting is said to starve down.

D.rationale: A beetle that uses only those seeds is a specialist.

hints: The passage says where masting is MOST pronounced. What is the opposite case?

strategy.explanation: Note the word LEAST, then reverse the passage's prediction.

candidates.remember: For LEAST/EXCEPT questions, find the rule and take its opposite.

author_checklist.hardness: Requires inverting the passage's stated prediction and recognizing a generalist from a description; three choices describe specialists in different words.

candidates.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 3, the word "pronounced" most nearly means:
candidates.evidence: masting should be most pronounced in species
candidates.explanation: Masting "most pronounced" means most marked or noticeable.

A.rationale: This is the familiar meaning, which does not fit a pattern in tree species.

D.rationale: The idea predicts masting; "pronounced" describes how strong the masting is.

hints: Substitute each choice into the sentence.
candidates.remember: Vocabulary-in-context: the familiar meaning is often the trap.

candidates.stem: According to paragraph 4, a tree that flowered heavily in a year when its neighbors did not would most likely:

choices.A: waste much of its effort, since little of the pollen in the air would reach its flowers.
choices.B: attract more seed predators than its neighbors, since its crop would stand out.
choices.C: produce more seeds than usual, since it would face less competition for pollen.
choices.D: be pollinated by insects instead of by wind, since the air would contain little pollen.

candidates.evidence: would waste much of the effort
candidates.explanation: With few neighbors flowering, the air holds little pollen, so wind pollination fertilizes few of its flowers and much of the effort is wasted.

B.rationale: Predators are discussed in paragraph 3, not as the problem in paragraph 4.

C.rationale: Paragraph 4 says heavy flowering alone wastes effort; it does not increase seed production.

D.rationale: Nothing suggests the pollination method changes.

hints: What happens to wind pollination when few trees flower?

strategy.explanation: Reread the last sentence of paragraph 4.

candidates.remember: Detail questions: match the reason the passage gives, not one from another paragraph.

candidates.stem: Paragraphs 3 and 4 differ from paragraph 5 in that paragraphs 3 and 4 mainly explain:

choices.A: how trees coordinate the timing of masting, while paragraph 5 explains why masting benefits them.
choices.B: the history of research on masting, while paragraph 5 presents the author's own field observations.
choices.C: masting in oaks only, while paragraph 5 extends the explanation to every kind of tree.
choices.D: why masting benefits trees, while paragraph 5 explains how trees coordinate its timing.

candidates.evidence: Neither explanation tells us how trees spread across a region manage to act together
candidates.explanation: Paragraphs 3 and 4 give benefits (fewer seeds eaten, better pollination). Paragraph 5 opens by noting those explanations do not show how trees act together, then offers weather as the coordinating cue.

A.rationale: This reverses the roles of the paragraphs.

B.rationale: No paragraph reports the author's own observations.

C.rationale: Paragraph 4 already says "like many masting trees," and paragraph 5 does not claim all trees.

hints: What question does the first sentence of paragraph 5 say is still open?

strategy.explanation: Label each paragraph's job: why or how?

candidates.remember: Watch for choices that reverse the roles of two parts.

author_checklist.hardness: The near-miss reverses the why/how roles, and the distinction depends on the first sentence of paragraph 5.

candidates.stem: The last sentence of the passage mainly serves to:

choices.A: suggest that individual trees plan their seed crops several years in advance.
choices.B: warn that forests will decline sharply if mast years ever stop occurring.
choices.C: stress that masting is a shared pattern that developed over time without any plan.
choices.D: introduce a new hypothesis that researchers will need to test in the future.

candidates.evidence: It is an arrangement that no single tree designed
candidates.explanation: The closing sentence characterizes masting as a collective arrangement that emerged "over many generations" rather than by design.

A.rationale: The sentence says "no single tree designed" the arrangement.

B.rationale: "Depend on" describes a long-standing arrangement; no warning is given.

D.rationale: The sentence sums up the picture already described rather than proposing something new.

hints: What do "no single tree designed" and "over many generations" emphasize?
candidates.remember: Closing sentences often generalize the passage's point.

candidates.stem: The passage indicates that for most of the twentieth century, ecologists believed that mast years:

choices.A: resulted mainly from good or poor growing conditions.
choices.B: were triggered by rising numbers of seed-eating animals.
choices.C: occurred when distant trees signaled to one another.
choices.D: depended chiefly on how efficiently pollen spread.

candidates.evidence: they treated them largely as a matter of weather
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 1 says ecologists treated mast years "largely as a matter of weather": good seasons, big crops; bad seasons, small ones.

B.rationale: Seed predators appear only in the later alternative explanation.

C.rationale: Signaling between trees is never described.

D.rationale: Pollination is the second alternative, not the earlier view.

candidates.remember: Detail questions: the answer is restated, not invented.
